rows.en: Another enactment Yoḥanan made: until his days there was striking with the hammer in Jerusalem, and he abolished the matter. This enactment too, according to the view of the ancients, was made for the repair of religion. That is: until his days they were accustomed to permit work on the intermediate days of the festival, and Yoḥanan enacted that no work may be done on them. Yet from their mentioning "striking with the hammer" it appears that they thought Yoḥanan forbade only public work, such as striking with a hammer, whose sounds all the people hear; and therefore until his days they were accustomed to permit all kinds of work, and the intermediate days of the festival stood on the level of working days. But who knows whether they said this from an ancient tradition or from conjecture? Perhaps this was nothing but an enactment for the benefit of the inhabitants of the city, that no tumultuous noise be heard in the royal city. And what is the connection between this enactment and the time of Yoḥanan the High Priest? If the reason for the enactment is the benefit of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the sound of the hammer blows coming out of the workshops of the craftsmen who work in iron should not be heard in the royal city, did the hour not already require this before the time of Yoḥanan? But it seems that in truth it was already the custom of old that the smith and the metalworker had their dwelling outside the city, in the outskirts of Jerusalem; but in time of war, when the enemy was outside, the smith and the metalworker who made weapons of war fled into the city. For such was the custom in ancient days, that the conquering enemy removed every smith from the conquered land, lest they make sword or spear (1 Samuel 13:19); and so the king of Babylon exiled, together with the mighty men of valor, "the craftsmen and the smiths" [2 Kings 24:14]. Therefore in the days of the Hasmonean war they settled the ironsmiths inside the city, and there was striking with the hammer in Jerusalem, until Yoḥanan came, in whose days there was peace and security in the land, and he restored the matter to its former state. In regard to the divine service in the Temple, too, he made enactments. The first is that he abolished the "awakeners." For until his days the Levites said in song: "Awake, why do You sleep, O Lord" (Psalms 44). That psalm was composed in the days of the first wars that the Hasmoneans fought against Antiochus Epiphanes, who reviled and blasphemed the armies of God (verse 16⚠1); the pious were forced to go into the caves of the rocks [cf. Isaiah 2:19] and into the place of jackals (ibid. 20); for the sake of God's Torah they were killed all the day (23), and they were scattered among the nations and sold as slaves (12, 13). At that time many prayers were composed, and they have been preserved for us in the collection of the book of Psalms. And this is the psalm in which they prayed to God: "Awake, why do You sleep, O Lord!" This psalm was sung in the Temple all the days of the wars, until the days of Yoḥanan. But we already know that Yoḥanan, out of love of truth, refused to say anything before God that did not agree with the truth, and he abolished the declaration of the tithe because it was a thanksgiving not fitting for his time; so too he abolished the saying of "Awake, why do You sleep, O Lord," because in his days the sun of salvation shone upon them and they defeated their enemies, and he saw that this psalm no longer fitted his time (*Tosafot Ḥadashim* on Ma'aser Sheni ch. 5; *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11). Another enactment he made in the Temple service: formerly the custom was to cut the sacrificial animal between its horns, so that the blood would fall into its eyes and it would be easy to bind; and Yoḥanan abolished this custom, for he said that this was nothing but like inflicting a blemish on the holy offerings of the altar, since through the cutting one makes the offering terefah. But this reason too was not accepted among them, for some said that he abolished this custom because it is the custom of the nations in their sacrifices (Babylonian Talmud Sotah, and the Tosefta there, ch. 13). Perhaps he had no other reason than to spare the animal needless suffering, since it could be done in another way in which its suffering is not so great. And so he did in truth: in place of the cutting he enacted that they make rings in which to insert the animal's neck.{v1_07_14:1} — These are the enactments ascribed specifically to Yoḥanan the High Priest; but without doubt other enactments too were made in his time, to fix the nails of religion firmly as of old. And it seems very likely that a number of new statutes and laws that have come down to us concerning the Kutim [Samaritans] should be ascribed to his time. For like most of the nations around them, so the Kutim in their midst were a grief of spirit and thorns in the eyes of all the Jews. Therefore Yoḥanan stirred up his wrath to chastise them. He went up against Shechem, the dwelling place of the Kutim, captured it, and destroyed their temple on the top of Mount Gerizim after it had stood two hundred years; and this temple of theirs never rose again (*Antiquities* 3, 16⚠2). But the Kutim were not chastened by all this. The inhabitants of Samaria now did Israel even more harm, for their hatred had grown greater than it had been in earlier days. And Yoḥanan went up against Samaria and besieged it a full year. But he did not lead the war himself, for he was old and advanced in days, and at the head of the army he placed his two sons, Aristobulus and Antigonus. About the outcome of this war a legend spread in the generations after him: that Yoḥanan heard a heavenly voice coming out of the Holy of Holies, saying: "The young men who went to wage war have been victorious!" And they wrote down that hour, and it was found to match (Sotah 33a; Josephus, ibid.). Now whatever the value of this legend may be, at any rate we see how great Yoḥanan's honor was in the eyes of his people, so that they ascribed to him the rank of prophecy as well. But the war and the victory cannot but have been the cause of a number of enactments regarding the Kutim.

1.note: The verse on the reviler and blasphemer (מקול מחרף ומגדף) is Psalm 44:17 in the Hebrew numbering; kept as printed.

2.note: Printed as book 3 (ס"ג); the destruction of the Gerizim temple is in Antiquities book 13 (13.9.1). Probably for סי"ג.

rows.en: The Kutim, or Samaritans, were a mixed people, made up of Israelites who remained in Samaria and in other cities after the exile of the land by Sennacherib, and of the nations whom the king of Assyria settled in the land of Israel. Of their deeds until Judah's return from Babylon we have no established information, but we have some traces of them. The righteous kings who were in Judah endeavored to bring them truly into the covenant of the Lord. When Hezekiah made the Passover, he sent into their land and asked that they come to make the Passover. Many responded to his request, but many laughed at them and mocked them (2 Chronicles 30:10); and these mockers were without doubt of the Israelites who had made common cause with the nations that had settled in their midst. King Josiah too endeavored to do them good (ibid. 34). In the days of Jeremiah men came from Shechem, from Shiloh and from Samaria to bring an offering and frankincense to the house of the Lord (Jeremiah 41:5), and they were of the good ones. To Zechariah too came men from Bethel to ask about the fasts [Zechariah 7:2–3], and from the names of the men one may judge that they were not Israelites (Jost, p. 46). After the Jews returned from the exile, the Samaritans wished to join the Jews, to be one nation and to build with them a sanctuary to the Lord; but the Jews pushed them away with both hands and said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to the Lord" (Ezra 4:1–4). This rejection widened the separation, and from that time on they harassed Israel, informed against them before the government, and caused a great delay in the building of the Temple. The Jews did all in their power to keep them away and laid down harsh statutes against joining with the nations who had been settled in the land, although these assured them that they too, like them, would seek the God of Israel; they set it as a statute that shall not pass away: "Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons, and do not seek their peace or their good forever" (ibid. 9:12). But against this the Samaritans too exerted all the force of their strength and devised schemes to entice many of Israel to join them, and their desire succeeded in their hand; and not many days passed before they built themselves a temple on the top of Mount Gerizim and became a separate sect. Already at the time they built their sanctuary on Mount Gerizim they had a copy of the book of the Torah of Moses, and perhaps already in the first copy they made falsifications that are still found in their copy today; for on the basis of one falsification that they introduced into their Torah they endeavored to show that Mount Gerizim is the place that the Lord chose. Apart from the falsifications they differed from the Jews with regard to the Holy Scriptures also in this, that they had no Holy Scriptures at all except the Torah of Moses and the book of Joshua. But their corrupt opinion in these matters caused the Jews too to make fences and hedges on their side, as we have already seen above (chs. 7 and 10). In the principles of faith, too, they differed from the Jews, for they did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, and according to the report of the Talmud this was so already among the first Kutim (Berakhot ch. 8, and Rashi's commentary there). And without doubt they differed from the Jews in other matters touching religion as well; for if they were so strict about keeping them away that they forbade intermarriage with them, this is a sign that they regarded them as the peoples of the land. And all that is known of their affairs from the beginning of the coming of the Greeks in the wake of Alexander bears witness that as their status was then, in the days of Ezra, so was their status afterward, in the days of Alexander; no compromise was made between them and the Jews, but the separation grew wider and wider. From the words that Ben Sira said about them (50:25–26) it also appears that they were regarded as the peoples of the land. But we have no reliable evidence about particular enactments that should be ascribed to that time. From the days of the Maccabees, however, there was great reason to lay down statutes concerning their affairs. For until that time they were at any rate, to outward appearance, a branch of the believers in the Torah of Moses; but in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes they removed the veil from their faces and revealed what was in their heart. Then they were in great fear lest the cup of staggering pass over them too, as over the Jews; so they came before Antiochus and declared that they were not Jews at heart, that they did not keep the Sabbath and the festivals with a willing soul, and that they wished to worship the gods of the Greeks and to dedicate their temple to them (*Antiquities* 12, 5). After such a confession, who would regard them as faithful to the religion of Moses? Of this the ancient proverb says: "Sorry is the dough when its own baker testifies that it is bad." Therefore, from the state of religion too, Yoḥanan had no reason to spare them.{v1_07_15:1} Indeed, if we consider the affairs of Yoḥanan and his enactments, we find that great was the effort he made for the repair of religion; therefore there is no doubt that after he had subdued the Kutim he also set his heart to make religious enactments regarding them. As the sanctuary on Mount Gerizim had been thorns in their eyes while it stood, so they rejoiced at the news of its destruction, and therefore they made that day, the seventeenth of the month of Kislev (another reading: 540⚠1), a day of rejoicing and festival (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 8). But even after its destruction the Jews did not try to win the Samaritans over with words of goodwill, so that they would now bring their offerings to the Temple in Jerusalem. Rather the opposite: it was then that they made it a statute that obligatory offerings are not to be accepted from the Kutim (Sheqalim 1:8⚠2). One decree that the later [sources] ascribed to Ezra, that a man may not eat the bread of the Kutim (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer ch. 38), and that "whoever eats the bread of the Kutim is like one who eats pork" (Shevi'it 8:10), was perhaps also a decree of Yoḥanan the High Priest and the sages of his time; for only in his time were the Kutim regarded by them as worse than full gentiles, and therefore they decreed even against their bread, although the bread of gentiles had not yet been forbidden in those days (Shabbat ch. 1). Later, however, they regarded them as true converts, as is found in various places; in the days of R. Meir they sought to decree against them, and [the others] would not agree to the decree, until in the days of the Amoraim they made them like full gentiles.{v1_07_15:2}

1.note: Meaning of ג"א unclear; read as גירסא אחרת ('another reading') with the number 540. It may also be a date.

2.note: The rule that offerings are not accepted from a Kuti is Mishnah Sheqalim 1:5 (Weiss himself cites 1:5 in note 2). Kept as printed.

rows.en: The chief reason why the temple of the Kutim was a grief of spirit to the Jews was that they did not give the Temple in Jerusalem the honor due to it, and said that the place the Lord chose is not in Jerusalem, but Mount Gerizim is the chosen place, and their temple is the house that the Lord desired to make His dwelling there. This aroused the hatred of the Jews against them from the beginning of the founding of their temple until its destruction. Even if these Kutim had not harassed them with their plots at all times and in every way, this matter alone — that they raised the rank of their temple above the rank of the Temple in Jerusalem — was enough for their hatred to stay fixed, never to be wiped out. Therefore it was this matter alone that made their separation a complete separation, not their deviation from the accepted understanding of some statutes and from the manner of their observance among the Jews. Now we will understand why the temple in Egypt was not likewise a cause of separation between the Jews in the land of Israel and the Jews of Alexandria. For in Egypt too the Jews who lived there built a temple to God. This temple was called the House of Onias. It was founded in the days when King Ptolemy Philometor reigned over Egypt. Then Onias, of the priestly seed and of the descendants of Simeon the Just, fled to Egypt, because his soul loathed the oppressor, Antiochus Epiphanes. There he found favor in the eyes of King Ptolemy and his wife Cleopatra — and according to some (Ewald vol. 4, p. 409; Graetz vol. 3, p. 35) he became commander over the king's armies — and he received permission from the king to build a temple in Egypt. At the beginning of this temple's days there was great turmoil in the land of Israel, and the hour was not free to pay attention to events in a distant land; therefore without doubt they took no notice of the matter. Besides, there was no need to take notice, for the building of this house was not evil in the eyes of the leaders in the land of Israel. For the Alexandrians, though they honored with reverence the temple they had built, did not on that account cease to turn their eyes and their heart to holy Jerusalem; they thought and believed that the Temple in Jerusalem is the place that the Lord chose to make His dwelling there, and to it they lifted up their soul. There they sent their freewill gifts, and from time to time offerings too. That being so, they themselves did not regard their temple as equal in value to the Temple in Jerusalem, but only as a great high place. Therefore in no way was this house a cause of separation between the Jews in the land of Israel and the Jews of Alexandria. And since the Jews in the land of Israel regarded the house in Alexandria at any rate as a minor sanctuary, it is self-evident that it was necessary to define the law of this house, its rules and its sanctity: with regard to dedications made without specification, does the one who dedicates fulfill the vow he vowed when he brings the dedicated offering to the House of Onias? And so they were compelled to define other matters like this. It seems that the most fitting time for defining statutes in this matter was the time of Yoḥanan. For then they had relief on every side, and not only was the hour free for it, but the hour demanded it. For his time was a time of new foundation for the Torah, and religion renewed its youth like the eagle [Psalms 103:5], to be strengthened by firmly planted nails [Ecclesiastes 12:11]. And especially, after we have seen that Yoḥanan endeavored to destroy the Kutim from the land, that it was decreed that they be worse than the gentiles, and that they destroyed their temple, they were therefore compelled to speak also of the house in Alexandria: to distinguish it from the house that the Kutim had, and to make known that even if its value is not like the value of the house in Jerusalem, it is at any rate regarded as a high place consecrated to the Lord. But of their enactments concerning this house we have only a few remnants. The first halakhah on this point is: "One who says, 'I take upon myself a burnt offering,' shall offer it in the Temple; and if he offered it in the House of Onias he has not fulfilled his obligation" (Menaḥot 109b). By this they wished to make known that those living in Egypt still have obligations that bind them to the Temple in Jerusalem: that we should not think that the temple in Egypt would be for the inhabitants of the land of Egypt what the Temple in Jerusalem is for the inhabitants of the land of Israel; rather, the essence of holiness depends on Jerusalem for all Israel, wherever one's place of dwelling may be. Therefore they made it a statute that for the inhabitants of Egypt too the Temple in Jerusalem is the main thing, and for this reason whatever a man of Israel dedicates to the altar without specification, in whatever place it may be, he is obliged to bring to Jerusalem. And another halakhah they taught: "One who says, 'I take upon myself a burnt offering that I will offer in the House of Onias,' shall offer it in the Temple; and if he offered it in the House of Onias he has fulfilled his obligation." Thus, although he said explicitly that he would offer it in the House of Onias, he should nevertheless offer it in the Temple, since by right all vows and freewill offerings should be brought to the Temple in Jerusalem, which is the main thing. But if he did as he specified in his vow and offered it in the House of Onias, he has also fulfilled his vow. A similar halakhah was taught regarding Nazirite vows. The idea underlying these halakhot is this: although they endeavored to hold fast the cord binding the members of the nation in all the lands of their dispersion, so that their eyes and heart would always be turned only to the one point, namely the Temple in Jerusalem, and surely in their heart they were not pleased with the House of Onias, nevertheless, since they had built this house there to the name of the Lord, the sages in the land of Israel did not wish to turn their good intention into evil and to count their deeds as rebellion and trespass against the Lord. Therefore they permitted offering in this house, although the law of the Torah forbade all offering outside the Temple and warned with the penalty of karet every man who offers up a burnt offering or sacrifice outside the Lord's sanctuary [Leviticus 17:8–9]; and they acted against the statute because they saw that the hour required it. And how right are the words of one of the later [sages] (Rava), when he says: "This one intended a gift; he said: if the House of Onias suffices for me, I take the trouble to bring it, but more than this I do not wish to do, for I cannot trouble myself to go on a long journey." Now just as this justification sufficed for the private individual who dedicated his offering, so it is a sufficient justification for the early sages for not questioning the very founding of the house in Egypt and its establishment: since they intended the honor of the Lord and established it because the way was far from them, so that if this house sufficed for them, good, and if it did not suffice them, they would wholly neglect the service of offerings; and on this account the sages made no complaint against them. And it is very surprising that they spoke only of vowed and freewill offerings, and there is no speech nor words [Psalms 19:4] about obligatory offerings of the community or of the individual; this is a sign that offering in their temple was not regarded as forbidden even by the sages in the land of Israel. It is plain that their aim was only to lay down a statute regarding vows and freewill offerings, so that their table should not be full and the table of the house of God in Jerusalem empty.{v1_07_17:1} Yet although, for the sake of wisdom and peace, they were compelled to agree to what they had no power to change, there is no doubt that they held a grudge in their heart. For this reason they used to penalize the priests who had served in the House of Onias, that they should not serve in the Temple. But this penalty too was made with fairness: they penalized them only in that they did not let them approach the altar of the Temple to offer, but they did not curtail their livelihood; rather, they shared and ate the holy things with their brothers the priests (Menaḥot 109a). Whether all these enactments that came to light in the days of Yoḥanan, some of which are mentioned specifically by his name, all came out with the agreement of all the sages of the Torah among the Pharisees, we are not told explicitly; but it seems that it was so. For one enactment that he made was against the will of the sages, and it is mentioned specifically that it was against their will, and Yoḥanan too retracted it on this account; this is a sign that they did not dispute his other enactments. This enactment is told as follows: The Greek kingdom issued a decree that the name of Heaven not be mentioned on their lips; and when the Hasmonean kingdom prevailed and defeated them, they enacted that the name of Heaven be mentioned even in documents, and they would write: "In year such-and-such of Yoḥanan, high priest to God Most High." There is no doubt that this enactment was made in the days of Yoḥanan, for before him, in the days of Simeon, it was not so. In the days of Simeon they wrote "In year such-and-such of Simeon being high priest," and did not write "to God Most High" (Graetz vol. 3, p. 470). And before Simeon they did not count by the years of the high priest; only then, when they appointed Simeon as nasi, did they establish and take upon themselves that all letters and notes be written in his name and that they count by the year of his rule (1 Maccabees ch. 14, and *Antiquities* 12, ch. 6⚠1). But before that, when the hand of the Greeks was strong over them, they wrote and counted by the Greek kings and wrote the name of the ruler in documents (Yadayim 4:8). Therefore the enactment to write "high priest to God Most High" came out in the days of Yoḥanan; but it was not to the liking of the sages, for when the sages heard of the matter they said: "Tomorrow this one pays his debt, and the document is found thrown on a dunghill," and they abolished the matter, and they made that day a festival (Rosh Hashanah 18b). This day was the third of Tishri, and it is mentioned among the days on which one may not eulogize or fast (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 6). Now without doubt the Pharisee sages agreed to all his other enactments. This agreement was not disturbed until the end of his life; but until that time he cleaved to the Pharisees and was a strong support for establishing religion on its original foundation according to the opinions of the Pharisees. Therefore on the whole the days of his reign were good for Israel also with regard to restoring religion to its former state, and the time was fit for the study of the Torah and its development; and then too the eshkolot [the pairs of sages], which had ceased at the death of Yose ben Yo'ezer, returned.

1.note: Simeon's appointment is in Antiquities book 13 (13.6.7); book 12 looks wrong. Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: Geiger, in his book mentioned above [*Urschrift*], p. 178, thinks that in the halakhah of the Talmud too there is a memory of this old halakhah, and he brings the baraita of Sifrei Re'eh, piska 72: "R. Yose says: One might think that they are liable only for ṭevel from which nothing at all has been separated; whence [do we know that if] terumah was separated from it but first tithe was not separated from it; first tithe, but second tithe was not separated from it; second tithe, but the poor man's tithe was not separated from it — whence etc." And it is proved from his language that he speaks of three tithes in one year. But I deliberately left out this proof, because even if we say that there is in it a memory of an old halakhah that deviates from the new, there is still no proof in what respect it deviates: whether, as Geiger says, the old [halakhah] held that in the third year there are three tithes, or it deviates in this, that it held that in the third year there are two tithes, except that it is not second tithe that is set aside but first tithe, and in the third year one gives second tithe and the poor man's tithe, as in the first assumption of the Sifrei, piska 109 there; for in this way too the language of the Sifrei in piska 72 is well explained. The second proof he brings is from Sifrei 302: "'In the third year' etc. — one might think that two tithes apply in it; I have only the poor man's tithe, of which Scripture speaks; whence to include the other tithes?" And the meaning according to him is: one might think that only two tithes apply, or only the poor man's tithe alone; Scripture says "all" etc. [Deuteronomy 26:12] — it included [them]. But I have not found anywhere in the Sifrei or the Sifra or the Mekhilta a passage that says "one might think" and "I have only" one right after the other; for these two expressions indicate that it means: from this verse I would have said such-and-such. Now if it says "one might think that it speaks of two tithes," how can it say at once "I have from the verse only one tithe"? Necessarily there is an omission here, and it should read as there, in piska 109.

See Part Two of this work of ours, where we have conjectured a new reason for this enactment and have shown that in truth a custom close to this existed among the Greeks; and true and right is what they said about this in the Talmud, that this is the way of idolatry. See there well.

It is not our purpose to tell of the history of the Kutim, their character and their faith. R. Raphael Kirchheim in his book *Karmei Shomron* went deep into this subject with upright and wise words; some of his words served me as a guide. Jost too treated it at length in his book *Geschichte des Judenthums und seiner Secten*, vol. 1, p. 44 ff.

On the laws in which the Kutim are equal to Israel, see Berakhot 7:1; Demai 3:4, 5:9, 7:4; Terumot 3:9 (see Niddah 4:5). And there are mishnayot in which the Kutim are like gentiles; see Berakhot 8:8; Sheqalim 1:5; (Oholot 9:3?); Ṭohorot 5:8. All of these are anonymous, and they are old halakhot, from the time of Yoḥanan onward; and the former were taught afterward, when they made the law of the Kutim more lenient. In this way a resolution is found for a number of apparent contradictions. See Ḥullin (13a): "his bread (of a min) is the bread of a Kuti," and the Tosafot there; and there (4a), Tosafot s.v. matzat Kuti. Now in the name of R. Eliezer they said: "Whoever eats the bread of the Kutim is like one who eats pork"; and R. Akiva said: "Be silent, I will not tell you what R. Eliezer said," that is, that R. Eliezer was very lenient. If so, is there not a contradiction in what they received from R. Eliezer? But it is not so. For it is known that R. Eliezer is the master of old halakhot, and he received this tradition, that one who eats the bread of a Kuti is like one who eats pork, whose basis, in my opinion, lies in the time of Yoḥanan and in reliance on the story in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, except that there one must read Yoḥanan in place of Ezra. But what R. Akiva said in the name of R. Eliezer refers to R. Eliezer's own opinion about the Kutim of his time, whose law they had made lenient. Perhaps this was because, from the time of the war at the end of the days of the Temple, the Kutim joined the Jews against the Romans, so that the hatred between the two sides then ceased. See also *Karmei Shomron*, p. 10.
